title: The Twelve Networking Truths
summary: An April 1st humor RFC listing the fundamental truths of networking, such as things that cannot be fixed by more effort. It is satire.

plainLanguage.summary: A funny list of unavoidable facts about computer networks, written as a joke. It says things you cannot change no matter how hard you try.

questions: what are the twelve networking truths
what does rfc 1925 say about simplicity
subtitle: Twelve fundamental truths and paradoxes of network design.

tldr.problem: Networking engineers face repeated patterns of difficulty, including constraints that cannot be overcome by effort or resources, and design choices with unavoidable trade-offs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists 12 fundamental truths about networking, from the physical laws that constrain systems (speed of light, human gestation) to practical realities (the cost of complexity, the impossibility of universal solutions) and design wisdoms (preferring simplicity).
tldr.outcome: This is an April 1st humor RFC that codifies universal experiences in networking as if they were fundamental laws. The truths guide designers toward accepting constraints and embracing simplicity.

today: RFC 1925 is an April 1st joke document that has become a beloved part of Internet culture. The truths remain remarkably applicable to networking challenges decades later, offering both humor and genuine wisdom about the constraints and trade-offs inherent in network design.

sections.title: The Fundamental Truths
sections.content: RFC 1925 is an April 1st memo that documents the Twelve Networking Truths. The first truth is simply "It Has To Work," the fundamental requirement. The second truth invokes a physical law: no amount of effort can increase the speed of light, and therefore communication latency is a hard constraint. It includes a corollary that you cannot make a baby faster than nine months, acknowledging that some constraints of human nature cannot be overcome by additional effort.
sections.plainLanguage: The first truth is that the network must work. The second is that light only travels so fast, so you can never send a message faster than the laws of physics allow.

sections.title: Complexity, Trade-offs and Indirection
sections.content: Subsequent truths address design reality. Truth 3 notes that with enough thrust, pigs can fly (a playful metaphor for doing unlikely things), but this does not mean it is a good idea. Truth 5 states that multiple problems can always be combined into a single interdependent solution, but this is usually a mistake. Truth 6 says it is easier to move a problem around in the architecture than to solve it, with a corollary that you can always add another layer of indirection. Truth 7 notes that something always goes wrong, and good, fast, and cheap are only achievable two at a time. Truth 8 asserts that everything is more complicated than expected.
sections.plainLanguage: Some truths say you can always make things more complicated, or move problems instead of solving them. Another says everything takes longer than you think and costs more than you budget.

sections.title: Resources, Universality and Perfection
sections.content: Truth 9 declares that whatever the resource, you always need more. Truth 10 states that one design never fits all cases. Truth 11 warns that old ideas come back with new names regardless of whether they work. Truth 12, the final and most design-focused truth, says that in protocol design, perfection is reached not when there is nothing left to add, but when there is nothing left to take away. This truth champions simplicity and elegance in design.
sections.plainLanguage: You always need bigger and better computers. Nothing works for everyone. Old bad ideas keep being proposed with new names. And the best designs are as simple as possible.
